LLM API Pricing Calculator

Compare the monthly dollar cost of calling different LLM APIs for your own workload -- fresh input, cached input, and output tokens priced separately, using the rates you paste in from each provider's own pricing page.

Bring your own rates. This tool does not fetch or assert any provider's current price. Paste the input, cached-input, and output rates from each vendor's own pricing page, current today, and verify before you commit spend. The preloaded numbers below are illustrative examples, not current prices.

Why cached tokens usually dominate an agentic workload's bill

This calculator vs. a blended per-token estimate -- how far off one flat $/M rate can land.

Already have a usage log? The LLM Usage Log Analyzer shows where your actual bill went.

Comparing a subscription AI coding plan instead of raw API usage? See the AI Coding Plan vs. API Cost Calculator.

Paying for compute by the hour as well? The AWS commitment break-even calculator finds how much to commit to from your own usage curve.

1. Monthly token workload

The tokens you send and receive each month -- the same for every provider, since the workload doesn't change, only the rate it's billed at.

2. Provider rates ($ per million tokens)

Name each provider and paste in its currently quoted input, cached-input, and output rates from that provider's own pricing page. Leave a row's name blank to drop it from the comparison. Common questions

Why does this calculator ask for cached input tokens separately from fresh input?

Because modern LLM APIs bill them at very different rates. A cached input token — one the provider has already processed recently, such as a repeated system prompt or the prior turns of an agentic loop — is commonly billed at a fifth to a tenth of the fresh-input rate. Agentic and long-context workloads that resend the same context on every turn can have cached tokens be the majority of all billed input, so a single blended "$X per million input tokens" estimate can be badly wrong for exactly the workloads where cost matters most. See why cached tokens usually dominate an agentic workload's bill.

Why doesn't this calculator show live Claude, GPT, or Gemini prices?

Because a wrong number is worse than no number, and API pricing changes often. This calculator does the arithmetic — multiplying your token volumes by the rates you paste in — from each provider's own current pricing page. It never fetches or asserts a vendor's price on its own.

What is a reasonable cached-input rate to use?

There is no single correct number and it varies by provider and by cache mechanism (prompt caching, context caching, implicit vs. explicit caching). Check the provider's own current pricing page for its cached/cache-read input rate, and use that — the example rates preloaded on this page are illustrative starting points, not a claim about any provider's current price.

Does this calculator upload my token counts or rates anywhere?

No. Every field runs in your browser; nothing is sent to a server. An optional anonymous local counter records which buttons get used, never the numbers you typed, and can be turned off.

vs-a-blended-per-token-rate.html.text:
← LLM API Pricing Calculator

This calculator vs. a blended per-token estimate

"Multiply my monthly tokens by the $/M rate on the pricing page" is a one-line estimate. It also assumes every input token is billed the same, which is the assumption cached-token pricing exists to break.

What each approach actually involves

The blended estimate takes one rate -- almost always the fresh-input rate, since that is the number a pricing page leads with -- and multiplies it by the whole month's input tokens, cached and fresh lumped together, then adds output cost. One rate, one multiplication, done.

This calculator takes the same fresh-input, cached-input, and output rates a pricing-page lookup gives you and asks for the month's fresh input, cached input, and output tokens as three separate figures, then prices each token class at its own rate for up to four providers at once.

Worked exampleBlended (fresh rate on everything)This calculator (split by token class)
5,000,000 fresh input + 45,000,000 cached input + 2,000,000 output tokens/month, at $3.00 / $0.30 / $15.00 per million$180.00/month — 50,000,000 input tokens × $3.00, plus $30.00 output$58.50/month — $15.00 fresh input + $13.50 cached input + $30.00 output

These are the calculator's own default inputs and the Anthropic (Claude) example row preloaded on the calculator page, so you can load them there and check the arithmetic yourself. Blending overstates this workload by $121.50/month -- about 3.1x the real total -- entirely from billing 45,000,000 cached tokens at the fresh rate instead of the cached rate. That gap tracks the workload's cached share directly: at 90% cached input (this example's share), most of the bill is the rate the blended estimate got wrong. See why prompt caching changes the math for why that share runs high on agentic and long-context workloads specifically.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want a provider's current fresh-input, cached-input, or output rate.The provider's own pricing page — this calculator never fetches or asserts that for you.
I just want a rough monthly ceiling and don't know or care about my cache share.A blended estimate is fine as a ceiling — it is usually an overstatement, not an understatement, of the split total.
I want to compare providers, or know what caching is actually worth on my workload.This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

What is the blended-per-token shortcut this page compares against?

Taking a provider's headline $/million-token rate -- almost always the fresh-input rate, since that is the number a pricing page leads with -- and multiplying it by the month's total input tokens, cached and fresh together, then adding output cost on top. It is a one-line estimate: no separate cache rate, no split, one multiplication.

How much can a blended estimate overstate the bill?

On this calculator's own default example workload (5,000,000 fresh input, 45,000,000 cached input, 2,000,000 output tokens per month) at Anthropic's example rates ($3/M fresh input, $0.30/M cached input, $15/M output), the split calculation totals $58.50/month. Blending -- billing all 50,000,000 input tokens at the $3 fresh rate -- totals $180.00/month, about 3.1x the real figure and $121.50/month higher, entirely from treating cached tokens as if they were fresh.

Does a blended rate always overstate cost, or can it understate it too?

It depends which single rate gets picked, and a headline rate is the fresh-input rate far more often than not, so overstating is the common direction. Picking the cached rate instead and applying it to fresh tokens too would understate the bill -- but that requires already knowing the cached rate exists and choosing to (wrongly) apply it everywhere, which is not the shortcut anyone reaches for by habit. Either way, the fix is the same: stop picking one rate and use each token class's own rate.

Does this page assert any provider's actual cache discount?

No. The $3.00 / $0.30 / $15.00 example rates above are the same illustrative placeholders preloaded on the calculator page, not a claim about Anthropic's or any provider's current pricing. Paste in each provider's own current rates from its pricing page before relying on either number.

why-prompt-caching-changes-the-math.html.text:
← LLM API Pricing Calculator

Why prompt caching changes the math

A blended “$X per million input tokens” estimate is one number. What a sustained agentic workload actually pays is usually mostly cache reads, billed at a fraction of that rate — here is why, and how to account for it.

What caching is, and why it exists

Modern LLM APIs let a provider avoid reprocessing input tokens it has already seen recently — a system prompt, a long document, or the earlier turns of a multi-step agentic conversation. Instead of billing those repeated tokens at the full input rate every single time, the provider bills them at a steep discount, commonly a fifth to a tenth of the fresh-input rate, because serving them from a cache costs the provider far less compute than processing them fresh. Different providers call this different things (prompt caching, context caching, cache reads and writes) and structure the discount slightly differently, but the shape is the same: some fraction of input is fresh, some fraction is a cache hit, and the two are billed at different rates.

Why this fraction is usually large for agents, not small

A one-shot question-and-answer call has little to cache -- most of its input is new every time. An agentic loop is the opposite case: a coding assistant, a tool-using agent, or a long chat session typically resends the entire conversation and tool context on every turn, appending only a small amount of new content each time. Nearly all of that resent context is identical to what was just sent a moment ago, so it is eligible for the cache discount on every subsequent turn. The cached share tends to grow as a session runs longer, not shrink -- the accumulated history is what gets resent, and it only gets longer.

This is not a small effect. Publicly reported figures from real, sustained agentic-coding sessions describe cache reads making up well over 90% of total input tokens across a session. At that share, the cached rate -- not the fresh-input rate most pricing pages headline -- is the number that actually determines most of the bill.

What this means for estimating cost

Estimating cost from total input tokens times one blended rate silently picks a rate to apply to the whole total, and that rate is usually either the fresh rate (overstating the bill, often badly, for an agentic workload) or a rate assumed from someone else's cache share (which may not match yours). The fix is not a better blended number -- it is not blending at all: track fresh and cached input tokens as separate figures, and price each at its own rate. That is the whole reason the LLM API Pricing Calculator asks for them separately rather than asking for one input-token total.

This page describes a general, widely documented mechanism common to current LLM APIs. It is not a claim about any specific provider's current cache discount, cache duration, or pricing -- check the provider's own pricing page for those.

Common questions

What is prompt/context caching in an LLM API?

A way for a provider to avoid reprocessing input tokens it has already seen recently — a system prompt, a long document, or the earlier turns of a multi-step agentic conversation. Instead of billing those repeated tokens at the full input rate every time, the provider bills them at a steep discount, because serving them from a cache costs the provider far less compute than processing them fresh.

Why do cached tokens dominate an agentic workload's bill?

An agentic loop — a coding assistant, a tool-using agent, a long chat session — typically resends the entire conversation and tool context on every turn, appending only a small amount of new content each time. Nearly all of that resent context is identical to what was just sent a moment ago, so it is eligible for the cache discount. Publicly reported real-world figures put cache reads at well over 90% of total input tokens for sustained agentic sessions, which makes the cached rate, not the fresh rate, the number that actually determines the bill.

Why does a single blended per-token rate get this wrong?

Because it assumes every input token costs the same, when in an agentic workload most of them are billed at a fraction of the fresh-input rate. Estimating cost from total tokens times one blended rate — often the fresh-input rate, since that is the headline number on a pricing page — overstates the bill for exactly the workloads it is most often applied to.
